Gynecology and urology · published research

Ovarian follicle maturation

Rodent studies report changes in follicle development and ovarian hormones, including more follicles and fewer cysts in a PCOS model. A small uncontrolled human study found a higher follicle count, but not a significant increase in retrieved oocytes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Rodent studies report changes in follicle development and ovarian hormones, including more follicles and fewer cysts in a PCOS model. A small uncontrolled human study found a higher follicle count, but not a significant increase in retrieved oocytes.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications were identified: one direct rat folliculogenesis experiment and three narrowly mapped ovarian studies of mature mice, PCOS rats, and aged mice. One mapped paper also included a 10-woman diminished-ovarian-reserve pilot and is summarized under ovarian aging; it is not a separate human replication. Follicle counts, oocyte competence, and completed maturation are related but distinct outcomes.

Human and clinical evidence

The mapped 10-woman single-arm study reported a rise in median antral follicle count, but retrieved-oocyte yield increased only nonsignificantly. It did not establish that PBM caused more mature oocytes, successful fertilization, or pregnancy. No controlled human trial directly measuring follicle maturation was identified (Su et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In a 28-rat comparison, ovarian irradiation with 810-nm near-infrared light produced greater follicular activity than 630-nm red light or clomiphene on several measured outcomes, including the number of oocytes. The authors described the results as a basis for further work rather than a treatment for human ovulatory disorders (Naseri et al. 2017).

Other mapped models reported more early-stage follicles and AMH-positive follicles in mature mice, and increased follicles and corpora lutea with fewer ovarian cysts in PCOS rats. The aged-mouse study found better ovarian measures with 630-nm red light, while its 850-nm arm did not show the same pregnancy and litter-size gains. These studies vary in age, disease model, wavelength, and outcome; their results should not be pooled as if they tested one protocol (Alves et al. 2019; Su et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate laboratory study directly testing maturation of isolated follicles was identified in this mapped set. Some included animal papers measured ovarian cells or oocyte-related markers as part of whole-animal experiments, which is not equivalent to a controlled human oocyte-maturation study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct rat study compared red visible light at 630 nm with near-infrared light at 810 nm, using 5 J/cm². The human pilot used an externally applied 630-nm red LED before egg retrieval. Other animal protocols used different doses and disease models. No consistent optimum has been established, and a wavelength or dose that changes rodent follicle counts cannot be assumed to improve human oocyte maturation.

Interpretation

The animal literature shows changes in follicle development and related ovarian measures, with some outcomes moving in the direction of greater follicular activity. The human evidence remains limited to a small, uncontrolled follicle-count observation without significant oocyte-yield improvement. A stronger conclusion requires controlled human studies that follow follicles through mature oocyte retrieval, fertilization, embryo development, pregnancy, and live birth.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for follicular and hormonal changes in rodent models Very low for human oocyte maturation and fertility outcomes
Publications and records4 relevant articles (1 direct and 3 narrowly mapped)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct rat study and related rodent experiments report changes in follicle stages, hormones, or oocyte quality, but they use different healthy, PCOS, and aging models. The small human study measured follicle count rather than proving mature-oocyte or live-birth benefit. Independent work with prespecified maturation, fertilization, embryo, and pregnancy outcomes would strengthen the assessment.
